sections.h2: What is the quickest way to part with a house in Duluth?
sections.html:
A Duluth owner can put the house on the market, skip the agent, or accept a cash bid from a buyer who takes the property untouched and closes when you say. Repairs, tenants, liens and your moving date decide which fits.

Duluth, in Gwinnett County, keeps adding people: the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 33,815, up from 31,873 at the 2020 count and 26,600 in 2010. Owners occupy 56.5% of homes, so sellers share the market with a large renter population.

Speed pays off when a roof, kitchen or foundation needs money you would rather not spend, when two mortgages are running at once, or when an estate must be wrapped up.

sections.h2: What do Census figures reveal about Duluth households?
sections.html:
Census five-year figures through 2024 show a middle home value of $400,800 and a middle household income of $95,331. Owners with a mortgage pay about $2,116 a month in ownership costs, and owners without one pay $678. Rent runs near $1,828.

Immigrants account for 30.9% of residents, and 38.3% of people over 5 speak another language at home. Buyers and tenants therefore come from many backgrounds, and a flyer in more than one language can widen your audience.

sections.h2: How did Duluth get its name and its start?
sections.html:
Duluth sits on land that was Cherokee territory until Gwinnett County was created in 1818. The city's history page says Evan Howell settled the area in 1821, and the crossroads he built became known as Howell's Cross Roads for about 40 years.

The railroad reached the town in 1871, and the name changed to Duluth in 1873 after Congress took up a bill about a railroad to Duluth, Minnesota. The state approved an official charter in 1876, and the city was formally incorporated in 1906. Duluth also elected Georgia's first female mayor, Alice Harrell Strickland, in 1922.

The city's seal still carries a steam engine and cotton, and a plan to restore the historic downtown was approved in 1998. For sellers, the old downtown core and the newer commercial corridor along Interstate 85 and Buford Highway are two different buyer pitches: walkable character in one, quick highway access in the other.

sections.h2: Which roads and landmarks help sell a Duluth house?
sections.html:
The city's own history page names Interstate 85, Buford Highway, Peachtree Industrial Boulevard, Georgia Highway 120 and Pleasant Hill Road as its main routes, and places Duluth about 25 miles northeast of Atlanta. Residents average 29.9 minutes getting to work, per the Census.

Highlight the features that match those routes:

  • Distance to Interstate 85 and the Pleasant Hill Road corridor for commuters.
  • Closeness to downtown events and the Southeastern Railway Museum for buyers who like a town-center setting.
  • Nearby parks and green space, since the city has been a designated Tree City since 1989 according to its history page.
  • Proximity to shopping and dining along the commercial corridors.

Be accurate about distances and school assignment, and let buyers confirm both for the exact address rather than quoting a boundary from memory.

sections.h2: Does Duluth bill its own property tax?
sections.html:
Yes. The city bills, collects and disburses its own property tax, apart from the Gwinnett County bill, using values from the county's Tax Assessor and a millage rate adopted by the City Council.

For tax year 2026 the city's page says notices went out at the end of September with a December 15, 2026 due date, and that any unpaid earlier-year amounts get added to that bill. The city also adds an annual stormwater fee to the bill: for 2026 it is $92.70 for most detached single-family homes and $46.35 for most condominiums and townhomes.

A new owner who has no city bill by October 15 is asked to contact the property tax office. When you sell, have the closing attorney check the city bill and the county bill separately, since each has its own payee.

sections.h2: How does a Gwinnett homestead exemption figure into a Duluth sale?
sections.html:
Gwinnett County's Tax Commissioner takes homestead applications for Duluth owners on a single form that covers every exemption. Primary residence status on January 1 is required, and an approved application filed otherwise applies to the following year.

The office takes applications all year, though the deadline printed on your Notice of Assessment controls whether it counts this year. Plan on 6 to 8 weeks for review. Once approved, an exemption renews itself unless something changes.

A fresh application is needed after turning 62, gaining a disability or veteran status, changing your name, or moving the deed into a trust. Whoever buys your house applies on their own after closing, so your exemption does not travel with the property.

sections.h2: What local events and sights give a Duluth address its appeal?
sections.html:
Duluth's home page promotes public art, Art Month, Fridays-N-Duluth, Howl on the Green and concerts, along with parks, dining and shopping. The history page adds the Southeastern Railway Museum, which preserves and operates historic railway equipment, and the Duluth Fall Festival, held the last weekend in September.

The city's history page credits the festival with more than 250 arts and crafts and food booths and crowds above 80,000. Buyers who like a lively calendar will respond to this, and a house within easy reach of downtown can lean on it. Quote only what you have confirmed yourself.

sections.h2: Which Duluth offices should I contact before selling?
sections.html:
The Planning and Development department covers permits, inspections, land use applications and ordinances, and the city code is posted online. If you have a half-finished addition, a deck built without a permit, or a stormwater matter pending, call that department before a buyer's inspector finds it.

The Planning Commission and Zoning Board of Appeals pages show whether a variance or rezoning is being discussed near your lot. The city clerk handles occupational tax and business applications, which matters if you run a business from the house.

Cash buyers still run a title review, so mention open permits, unpaid fees and violations at the start.

sections.h2: Is a cash bid or a listing the better call in Duluth?
sections.html:
Lean toward cash when speed and certainty outrank the last dollar. Lean toward a listing when the house is in good order and you can wait through showings, an inspection and a buyer's loan approval.

Ask every cash buyer for written terms covering price, closing costs, closing date and what follows if the buyer fails to close. Then estimate your take-home after the mortgage payoff, both tax bills and any liens, so you can set it beside a listing outcome.

If the house belongs to an estate or several owners, settle who may sign before anything else, since that question stalls more deals than any other.

faqs.q: When does Duluth's own tax bill come due?
faqs.a: The city set December 15, 2026 for tax year 2026, with notices mailed in late September. It publishes the dates each year on its property tax page.

faqs.q: Does a Duluth house carry both a city and a county tax bill?
faqs.a: Yes. The city bills its own tax and Gwinnett County bills separately, with the city drawing on county assessor values and a rate from its council.

faqs.q: What is the stormwater charge on a Duluth bill?
faqs.a: For 2026 the city lists $92.70 for most detached single-family homes and $46.35 for most condominiums and townhomes, printed on the tax bill.

faqs.q: How slow is a Gwinnett homestead review?
faqs.a: The county asks for 6 to 8 weeks. Filing is open all year, and the deadline on your Notice of Assessment governs the current year.

faqs.q: What does the Census list as a typical Duluth home value?
faqs.a: $400,800 is the middle value in the Census Bureau's five-year figures ending 2024. An individual house can price well above or below it.
